title: Yepun’s laser and the Magellanic Clouds
caption: Yepun's laser and the Magellanic Clouds, Paranal Observatory, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Paranal Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Ranked #63 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A powerful yellow laser beam shoots into the sky from Yepun, the fourth 8.2-meter Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope. To the left of the beam is the Large Magellanic Cloud and to the right the Small Magellanic Cloud, nearby dwarf galaxies easily seen with the unaided eye from the southern hemisphere.

The laser is there for a reason. Earth's atmosphere blurs everything ground-based telescopes observe, so astronomers use adaptive optics, in which computer-controlled mirrors change shape hundreds of times per second to cancel out the distortion.

The beam excites a layer of sodium atoms 90 km up, creating a glowing spot, an artificial star. Light returning from this Laser Guide Star is used as a reference to steer the deformable mirrors, giving images nearly as crisp as those a telescope in space would take.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph at ESO's Paranal Observatory, in visible light. The camera settings and color processing are not published.
understand.eye: A camera exposure can gather far more light than the eye, so the Magellanic Clouds and the beam may look brighter than they would to someone on site.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.

explore: Left of the Large Magellanic Cloud shines Canopus, the brightest star in Carina, and the one toward the upper right is Achernar, the brightest in Eridanus. Babak Tafreshi, an ESO Photo Ambassador, took the picture.
The VLT's Unit Telescopes carry names in Mapudungun, the Mapuche language. They are Antu (the Sun), Kueyen (the Moon), Melipal (the Southern Cross) and Yepun (Venus).
alt: A yellow laser beam rising from a telescope into a starry sky, with the two Magellanic Clouds on either side of it.
